content.investment_summary: NVIDIA is a full-stack accelerated-computing supplier built around GPUs and the CUDA software ecosystem. Q2 FY2027 revenue rose 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, including $89.0 billion from Data Center, while Oracle and Meta announced expanded deployment plans. The stock debate is whether that growth can remain durable despite concentrated customers, $279 billion of supply commitments and restrictions on China sales.
bear_case: Three direct customers represented 44% of H1 FY2027 revenue—16%, 15% and 13%—leaving results sensitive to purchasing decisions at a handful of counterparties.

Supply commitments reached $279 billion in July, versus $119 billion the previous quarter; long-term capacity agreements have already increased product costs, raising downside exposure if demand disappoints.
China access is impaired: NVIDIA says export controls have harmed its competitive position, while Chinese authorities encourage customers to buy domestic alternatives.
key_risks: Export controls, licensing decisions and Chinese procurement pressure could further restrict demand and shift customers toward domestic competitors.
Geopolitical disruption could interrupt NVIDIA’s Asia-concentrated supply chain despite October agreements targeting a 2.5× increase in substrate capacity over three years.
Customers’ internally developed alternatives could replace NVIDIA solutions and reduce demand for its products and services.
Data-center, energy and financing constraints could delay customer deployments, including Oracle’s planned multi-gigawatt expansion, and defer revenue.
bull_case: AI infrastructure spending remains powerful: Q2 FY2027 revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year, including $89.0 billion of Data Center revenue.
Oracle plans to expand Vera Rubin NVL72 systems to multi-gigawatt scale, while Meta plans broader deployments of NVIDIA processors and networking, supporting demand across the platform.
FY2026 generated approximately $96.7 billion of free cash flow—$102.7 billion of operating cash flow less $6.0 billion of capex—providing substantial self-funding capacity.
